# Summary bar graphs {#sec-sum-bar-graphs} ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="simple"} ## Theme: `theme_happymeal()` Graphs in this chapter use `fmggp2::theme_happymeal()`, modeled on a McDonald's Happy Meal box: red box, golden yellow marks, a cream plot area, and an Arial Rounded title. ::: :::: {.callout-note collapse="false" icon=false}
::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #02577A;"} **Requirements:** ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"} **✅ a numeric (continuous) variable** **✅ a categorical variable** ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="right"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](sum_bar_graphs_files/figure-html/full_code_display-1.png){fig-align='right' width=60% height=60%} ::: ::: :::: ## Description A summary bar graph has one bar for each group, where each bar is as high as one number that stands for that group,[^statistic] such as the mean. The groups go across the graph, and the numbers go up the side.[^axes] Each bar can also have a line that runs above and below its top, to show how much the numbers move around or how sure we can be about the bar.[^error-bars] In `ggplot2`, we can make summary bar graphs with `geom_bar()`. ## Set up ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **PACKAGES:** ::: Bring in the code we'll use.[^packages] ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} library(ggplot2) library(dplyr) # for tibble() and data manipulation library(tidyr) # for uncount() ``` ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **DATA:** ::: A Happy Meal is a box of food for a child from McDonald's, with a small toy to play with inside. In the last few years before 2000, McDonald's put a new toy in its Happy Meals every few weeks,[^promotion] and some toys (like the 1997 Teenie Beanie Babies) sold out at almost every McDonald's. We'll make up[^simulate] 28 days of Happy Meal sales at one McDonald's for four toys. Each toy gets its own average number sold in a day (`lambda`),[^rate] `tidyr::uncount()` makes one row for each day, and `rpois()` picks the number sold on each day.[^draw] Then we find the average number sold in a day for each toy (`avg_sold`). Starting with `set.seed()`[^seed] means you'll get the same 112 days every time you run the code below. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} set.seed(1997) # same 28 days of sales every time the code runs happy_meals <- tibble( promotion = c("Teenie Beanie Babies", "Furby", # four Happy Meal promotions "Hot Wheels", "Inspector Gadget"), lambda = c(420, 310, 220, 180) # average Happy Meals sold per day ) |> tidyr::uncount(28, .id = "day") |> # 28 days of each promotion mutate( promotion = factor(promotion, levels = unique(promotion)), # keep the order above sold = rpois(n(), lambda = lambda) # daily sales around each average ) |> select(promotion, day, sold) hm_sum_col <- happy_meals |> group_by(promotion) |> # one group per promotion summarise(avg_sold = mean(sold)) |> # average daily sales ungroup() dplyr::glimpse(hm_sum_col) #> Rows: 4 #> Columns: 2 #> $ promotion Teenie Beanie Babies, Furby, H… #> $ avg_sold 417.6071, 309.3929, 229.5714, … ``` ::: ::: ## Distribution A summary bar graph shows one number that stands for each group[^summary] (here, the mean). Each bar covers up 28 days of sales with one number, so it's worth knowing how much those days change before we trust the difference between two bars. Below we'll move from the sales on each day, to a graph, to the rule behind it.[^formula] ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **COUNT IT:** ::: Start with the first week of the Teenie Beanie Babies toy. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} head(happy_meals, 7) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: Sales on each day move up and down between about 400 and 450, but they never move far from the rate we gave `rpois()` (420). The table below shows the mean for each toy and how far a day usually falls from that mean.[^sd] It also shows how far each mean would usually move if we made up another 28 days (`se`).[^se] ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} hm_stats <- happy_meals |> group_by(promotion) |> summarise( mean = mean(sold), sd = sd(sold), se = sd(sold) / sqrt(n())) hm_stats ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **DRAW IT:** ::: The graph below puts the 28 days for each toy back behind its bar. The bar is the mean, each point is one day, and the line on each bar runs above and below the mean by two times how far the mean would usually move.[^two-se] The points reach farther from the mean for the toys that sold more, but the lines stay short because each mean comes from 28 days. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} ggplot(data = hm_stats, aes(x = promotion, y = mean)) + geom_col(aes(fill = promotion), show.legend = FALSE) + geom_jitter(data = happy_meals, aes(y = sold), width = 0.2, height = 0, alpha = 0.5, size = 1) + geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - 2 * se, ymax = mean + 2 * se), width = 0.3, linewidth = 0.8) + labs(x = "Toy promotion", y = "Happy Meals sold per day") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](sum_bar_graphs_files/figure-html/draw_sum_col-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **NAME IT:** ::: Each day's sales come from [a rule for how many times something happens at a set rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson_distribution),[^poisson] using the rate for that toy: $$ X \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda) $$ Under this rule, how far a day usually falls from the mean is $\sqrt{\lambda}$.[^poisson-sd] For Teenie Beanie Babies that's $\sqrt{420} \approx 20.5$ Happy Meals a day, and for the days we made up it's 21.8. The mean of $n$ days moves around much less; how far it usually moves is $\sqrt{\lambda / n}$:[^se-name] $$ \bar{X} \approx \text{Normal}\left(\lambda, \; \sqrt{\lambda / n}\right) $$ With $n = 28$ days, the Teenie Beanie Babies mean should land within about $2 \times \sqrt{420 / 28} \approx 7.7$ Happy Meals of 420. Our mean is 417.6. That's why we can trust the bars here: the differences between toys (100 or more Happy Meals a day) are much larger than the lines on the bars. Try cutting the 28 in `tidyr::uncount()` down to 3 days and watch the lines grow. ## Grammar ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **CODE:** ::: - Make the words around the graph[^labels] with `labs()` - Start the graph with `ggplot()` and give it `data` - Put `promotion` across the graph (`x`) and `avg_sold` up the side (`y`)[^map] - *Inside* the `aes()` of `geom_col()`, join `promotion` to `fill` so each bar gets its own color[^fill] - *Outside* the `aes()` of `geom_col()`, take away the key[^legend] with `show.legend = FALSE` ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} labs_sum_col <- labs( title = "Happy Meals", caption = "Simulated data", subtitle = "Average Happy Meals sold per day\nduring each toy promotion", x = "Toy promotion", y = "Average sold per day") ggp2_sum_col <- ggplot(data = hm_sum_col, aes(x = promotion, y = avg_sold)) + geom_col(aes(fill = promotion), show.legend = FALSE) ggp2_sum_col + labs_sum_col ``` ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **GRAPH:** ::: ::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](sum_bar_graphs_files/figure-html/create_graph_sum_col-1.png){width=100% height=100%} ::: ::: ## More info Below is more about how `geom_bar()` and `geom_col()` are different. ### Identity vs. Count - The `geom_bar()` way to show the data[^geom] can also make bar graphs by group, but we have to change `stat` to `"identity"`.[^identity] ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = hm_sum_col, aes(x = promotion, y = avg_sold)) + geom_bar(aes(fill = promotion), show.legend = FALSE, stat = "identity") + labs_sum_col ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](sum_bar_graphs_files/figure-html/show_stat_sum_col-1.png){width=100% height=100%} ::: ::: ::: ### `geom_bar()` vs. `geom_col()`
- `geom_bar()` will join a column of groups[^categorical] to `x` *or* `y` and show how many rows are in each group[^counts] (see [`stat_count()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_bar.html) for more) - `geom_col()` will join columns to *both* `x` *and* `y`,[^aesthetics] and we use it when we want to show a number for each group.[^numeric] `geom_col()` expects these numbers to be in their own column already (see [`stat_identity()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/stat_identity.html) for more) [^statistic]: A summary statistic, such as the mean or median. [^axes]: The categories go on the `x` axis, and the values go on the `y` axis. [^error-bars]: Error bars, which can show variation (such as the standard deviation) or confidence intervals. [^packages]: Install and load the packages. [^promotion]: A toy promotion. Each promotion is one group in the `promotion` column. [^simulate]: Simulate. [^rate]: The daily sales rate, which is the Poisson parameter $\lambda$. [^draw]: `rpois()` draws a random count from a Poisson distribution with that rate. [^seed]: Setting the random seed. [^summary]: A summary statistic (here, the mean). [^formula]: The formula. [^sd]: The standard deviation (`sd`). [^se]: The standard error of the mean (`se`). [^two-se]: Error bars that stretch two standard errors above and below the mean. [^poisson]: A Poisson distribution, which gives the number of times something happens in a fixed interval when it happens at a constant average rate. [^poisson-sd]: For a Poisson distribution, the variance equals $\lambda$, so the standard deviation is $\sqrt{\lambda}$. [^se-name]: The standard error of the mean. The formula below says the average of $n$ days is approximately normal, with mean $\lambda$ and standard deviation $\sqrt{\lambda / n}$. [^labels]: The labels (title, subtitle, caption, and axis titles). [^map]: Map `promotion` to `x` and `avg_sold` to `y` in `aes()`. [^fill]: Map `promotion` to the `fill` aesthetic. [^legend]: The legend. [^geom]: The `geom_bar()` geom. [^identity]: The `stat` argument. `"identity"` uses the `y` values as they are, instead of counting rows. [^categorical]: A categorical variable. [^counts]: Counts for the discrete levels. [^aesthetics]: The `x` and `y` aesthetics. [^numeric]: Numerical (quantitative) values across the levels of a categorical variable.
